items.text: git bisect run ./test.sh lets git binary-search your history for the commit that broke a test: exit 0 marks good, 125 skips, other codes up to 127 mark bad.
git reflog records everywhere HEAD has been, so commits 'lost' to a bad reset or rebase can be recovered with git reset --hard HEAD@{2}.
git worktree add ../hotfix -b hotfix origin/main checks out a new branch in a separate folder, so you can fix a bug without stashing current work.
git rebase -i HEAD~5 lets you reorder, squash, reword, or drop your last five commits before pushing them for review.
git commit --fixup=<sha> creates a 'fixup!' commit; git rebase -i --autosquash <base> then folds it into the target commit automatically.
git stash push -m 'wip parser' -- src/parser.py stashes only that path with a label, leaving your other changes in place.
git stash -u also stashes untracked files; plain git stash leaves new files behind in your working tree.
git blame -w -C -C -C ignores whitespace changes and follows lines moved or copied from other files, so blame points at the real author.
List mass-reformatting commits in .git-blame-ignore-revs and run git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs to hide them from blame.
git log -S 'functionName' (the pickaxe) finds commits that added or removed that string; git log -G 'regex' matches changed lines by regex.
git log -L :myFunction:src/app.py shows the history of a single function, commit by commit, with diffs.
git add -p stages changes hunk by hunk, so one messy working tree can become several focused commits.
git commit --amend --no-edit folds staged changes into the last commit without changing its message. Only amend commits you have not pushed.
git push --force-with-lease refuses to overwrite the remote branch if someone else pushed since your last fetch, unlike plain --force.
git switch -c feature creates and checks out a branch, and git restore file discards unstaged edits; both are clearer than the overloaded git checkout.
git diff --staged shows exactly what is about to be committed; plain git diff shows only unstaged changes.
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all draws a compact graph of every branch; save it as an alias with git config --global alias.lg.
git cherry-pick -x <sha> copies a commit onto your branch and appends '(cherry picked from commit ...)' to its message for traceability.
git config --global rerere.enabled true makes git record how you resolved a conflict and reapply that resolution when the same conflict recurs.
git config --global pull.rebase true makes git pull rebase your local commits instead of creating noisy merge commits.
git shortlog -sn --since='1 year ago' ranks recent contributors by commit count, showing who actually knows a codebase today.
git grep -n 'pattern' searches tracked files fast, and git grep 'pattern' v1.2.0 searches the code as it was at that tag.
git revert <sha> adds a new commit that undoes an old one, which is safe on shared branches where rewriting history is not.
git reset --soft HEAD~1 undoes the last commit but keeps its changes staged, ready to be split or reworded.
git diff main...feature (three dots) shows only what changed on feature since it branched from main, ignoring newer commits on main.
git fetch --prune deletes local references to remote branches that no longer exist; set git config --global fetch.prune true to always do it.
Sign commits with an SSH key: git config gpg.format ssh, point user.signingkey at your public key, then commit with -S (or set commit.gpgsign true).
Write commit subjects in the imperative and under about 50 characters, like 'Fix null check in parser', then explain why in the body.
Ctrl-R searches shell history as you type; press Ctrl-R again to cycle to older matches, Enter to run, or an arrow key to edit first.
!! repeats the previous command, so after a 'permission denied' you can just type sudo !!
!$ expands to the last argument of the previous command: after mkdir -p src/new/module, typing cd !$ moves into it.
Esc then . (or Alt-. with Option as Meta) inserts the previous command's last argument at the cursor; repeat it to cycle through older commands.
^old^new reruns the previous command with the first 'old' replaced by 'new', perfect for fixing a typo in a long command.
find . -name '*.log' -print0 | xargs -0 rm deletes files safely even when names contain spaces, because -print0 and -0 use NUL separators.
xargs -P 8 -n 1 runs up to 8 commands in parallel with one argument each: cat urls.txt | xargs -P 8 -n 1 curl -sO
jq '.items[] | {name, id}' extracts fields from JSON; add -r to print raw strings without quotes for use in shell scripts.
jq -r '.[] | select(.status == "failed") | .id' filters an array of objects by a field and prints the matching ids.
curl -s https://api.example.com/users | jq . pretty-prints and colors JSON, and fails loudly on invalid input, so it doubles as a validator.
fzf's shell integration binds Ctrl-T to paste a fuzzy-picked file path, Alt-C to cd into a directory, and replaces Ctrl-R with fuzzy history search.
ripgrep (rg) respects .gitignore and skips hidden and binary files by default, which makes it much faster than grep -r in big repos.
rg -t py 'def main' searches only Python files, rg -l lists just the matching filenames, and rg -C 3 shows 3 lines of context.
Ctrl-A and Ctrl-E jump to the start and end of the command line, Ctrl-W deletes the previous word, and Ctrl-K deletes to the end of the line.
fc opens your previous command in $EDITOR and runs it when you save and quit, ideal for fixing a long broken one-liner.
set -euo pipefail at the top of a bash script makes it exit on errors, on unset variables, and when any command in a pipeline fails.
Quote variables in shell scripts: write "$file" not $file, or a filename with spaces will be split into several arguments.
Run shellcheck on your shell scripts; it catches unquoted variables, broken conditionals, and other subtle bugs before they bite.
cmd > out.log 2>&1 sends stdout and stderr to the file; order matters, because cmd 2>&1 > out.log still prints errors to the terminal.
diff <(sort a.txt) <(sort b.txt) uses process substitution to compare command outputs without creating temporary files.
sort | uniq -c | sort -rn is the classic frequency count: pipe in one value per line and get the most common first.
Heredocs write multi-line files: cat <<'EOF' > config.yml ... EOF. Quoting 'EOF' stops the shell from expanding $variables inside.
watch -n 2 kubectl get pods reruns a command every 2 seconds and redraws the output; on macOS install it with brew install watch.
time <command> prints real, user, and sys time; real much larger than user + sys usually means the command is waiting on I/O or the network.
tail -f app.log follows a growing file, and tail -F keeps following even after the log is rotated and recreated.
In zsh, **/*.ts globs TypeScript files recursively, and *(.om[1,5]) matches the five most recently modified regular files.
Prefix a command with a space to keep it out of history (zsh: setopt HIST_IGNORE_SPACE, bash: HISTCONTROL=ignorespace), useful around secrets.
trap cleanup EXIT in a bash script runs your cleanup function however the script ends, so temp files never pile up.
Run long jobs inside tmux or screen so they survive a closed laptop lid or a dropped SSH connection; reattach later with tmux attach.
Cmd-Space opens Spotlight, which also does math, unit conversions, and definitions; Cmd-Return reveals the selected result in Finder.
Cmd-Shift-4 captures a selected area; press Space afterward to capture a whole window. Cmd-Shift-5 opens all screenshot and recording options.
Add Control to any screenshot shortcut, like Cmd-Ctrl-Shift-4, to copy the image to the clipboard instead of saving a file.
pbcopy and pbpaste bridge the terminal and clipboard: pbcopy < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub copies your public key, pbpaste | jq . formats copied JSON.
caffeinate -d keeps the display awake, and caffeinate -i ./long_job.sh prevents idle sleep only until that command finishes.
open . opens the current folder in Finder, open -a 'Visual Studio Code' notes.txt opens a file in a specific app, and open <url> opens the browser.
Press Cmd-Shift-. in any Finder window or file dialog to toggle hidden files, including dotfiles like .env and .gitignore.
Activity Monitor: sort the CPU or Memory tab by column to find hogs, and check the Energy tab for apps preventing sleep.
Cmd-Option-Esc opens Force Quit; from the terminal, pkill -f 'partial name' kills processes whose full command line matches.
mdfind queries the Spotlight index from the terminal: mdfind -name report finds files by name instantly, and mdfind -onlyin ~/dev term narrows the search.
In Finder or any file dialog, Cmd-Shift-G opens Go to Folder so you can type any path, including hidden ones like ~/Library.
Ctrl-Cmd-Q locks your Mac instantly; make it a habit every time you step away from your desk.
say 'build finished' speaks text aloud; chain it after long commands, like make && say done, so you can look away while you wait.
lsof -i :3000 shows which process is listening on port 3000, so you can find and kill the stray dev server holding it.
networkQuality (macOS 12+) measures upload, download, and responsiveness from the terminal to diagnose a slow connection.
Cmd-Shift-/ opens the Help menu search, which finds any menu command in the current app by name and shows where it lives.
brew bundle dump writes a Brewfile listing everything you installed with Homebrew; brew bundle install recreates that setup on a new Mac.
docker system df shows disk used by images, containers, volumes, and build cache; docker system prune reclaims space from stopped and dangling items.
docker logs -f --tail 100 <container> follows logs starting from the last 100 lines instead of dumping the entire history.
Order Dockerfile steps from least to most frequently changed: copy package manifests and install dependencies before COPY . . so the layer cache is reused.
Multi-stage Docker builds compile in a full SDK image and copy only the final artifact into a slim runtime image, often saving hundreds of MB.
A .dockerignore that excludes .git, node_modules, and build output speeds up builds and keeps local secrets out of the build context.
docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD":/work -w /work python:3.12 bash gives you a throwaway environment with the current folder mounted.
kubectl get pods -o wide adds node and pod IP columns, -w watches for changes live, and -A lists pods across all namespaces.
kubectl logs <pod> --previous shows logs from the last crashed container, which is where CrashLoopBackOff errors usually hide.
kubectl describe pod <pod> reveals image pull errors, OOMKilled, and failing probes; read the Events section at the bottom first.
kubectl port-forward svc/my-api 8080:80 makes a cluster service reachable on localhost:8080 without creating an ingress.
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=dev changes your default namespace so you can stop typing -n dev on every command.
kubectl rollout undo deployment/my-app rolls back to the previous revision; kubectl rollout history deployment/my-app lists revisions.
kubectl rollout restart deployment/my-app replaces pods gradually, e.g. to pick up a changed ConfigMap or Secret without downtime.
kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp lists recent events in time order, useful when pods will not schedule.
kubectl diff -f manifest.yaml shows what would change in the cluster before you run kubectl apply.
kubectl top pod shows live CPU and memory usage per pod (it requires metrics-server), which helps you tune requests and limits.
kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container> attaches an ephemeral debug container to a running pod that has no shell.
Exit code 137 means the process got SIGKILL (128 + 9); in containers that is usually the OOM killer, so check memory limits.
Rubber duck debugging works: explaining the code line by line, out loud, forces you to check the assumptions you skipped in your head.
Reproduce first: a reliable, minimal reproduction turns a mystery into a checklist, and it becomes your regression test once fixed.
Bisect more than commits: disable half the code, input data, or config, check whether the bug remains, and repeat until it is cornered.
Read the full stack trace: in Java the root cause is usually the last 'Caused by' section, and the first frame in your own code is where to start.
Conditional breakpoints pause only when an expression is true, like i == 999 or user.id == 42; right-click a breakpoint in most IDEs to add one.
VS Code logpoints and JetBrains non-suspending breakpoints print values without pausing or editing code, ideal for timing-sensitive bugs.
When a bug 'cannot happen', print the actual values, types, versions, and config in use; the wrong assumption is usually in one of them.
On Linux, strace -f -e trace=file ./app shows every file a program tries to open; on macOS, sudo fs_usage -w -f filesys shows file activity.
In Python, breakpoint() drops into pdb; there, 'where' shows the stack, 'pp var' pretty-prints a value, and 'c' continues.
Bugs that vanish when you add logging often signal race conditions or memory errors; run with -fsanitize=thread or -fsanitize=address to catch them.
A good unit test follows Arrange-Act-Assert and checks one behavior, and its name says what is broken when it fails.
Write the failing test before fixing a bug: it proves you reproduced the issue and keeps the bug from quietly coming back.
Flaky tests usually come from time, randomness, test ordering, or shared state; inject clocks and seeds instead of retrying until green.
Test behavior through public interfaces rather than private details, so refactoring does not break a pile of tests.
Mock the boundaries you do not own (network, clock, payment APIs), not every collaborator; over-mocked tests only test the mocks.
pytest -x stops at the first failure, --lf reruns only the tests that failed last time, and -k 'name' selects tests by keyword.
Coverage shows what is not tested, not what is well tested; 100% coverage with weak assertions can still miss obvious bugs.
Property-based testing (Hypothesis, fast-check, jqwik) generates hundreds of inputs and shrinks any failure to a minimal counterexample.
Keep pull requests small: review quality drops sharply beyond a few hundred lines, and huge diffs tend to get rubber-stamped.
Review your own diff before requesting review; you will catch leftover debug prints, stray TODOs, and unrelated changes.
In PR descriptions explain why, not just what: link the ticket, describe how you tested it, and flag the risky parts for reviewers.
Prefix review comments by weight, such as 'nit:', 'question:', or 'blocking:', so authors know what must change before merge.
Let formatters and linters in CI (Prettier, Black, gofmt) settle style debates, so human reviewers can focus on logic and design.
Log structured JSON with consistent keys like request_id, user_id, and duration_ms, so you can filter and aggregate instead of grepping.
Pass a correlation or trace ID through every service call and include it in each log line; it turns scattered logs into one request timeline.
Use log levels deliberately: ERROR needs action, WARN is unexpected but handled, INFO marks business events, and DEBUG stays off in production.
Never log secrets, tokens, passwords, or full card numbers; add redaction to the logger so one careless line cannot leak credentials.
EXPLAIN shows a query's plan; in PostgreSQL, EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs it and reports real row counts and timings for every step.
A composite index on (a, b) helps filters on a, or on a and b, but usually not filters on b alone: the leftmost-prefix rule.
Wrapping an indexed column in a function, like WHERE LOWER(email) = ?, blocks normal index use; add an expression index or store normalized values.
Avoid SELECT * in application queries: it fetches unneeded columns, prevents index-only scans, and can break code when columns change.
OFFSET pagination slows down on deep pages because skipped rows are still read; keyset pagination (WHERE id > :last ORDER BY id LIMIT 50) stays fast.
The N+1 query problem: loading 100 rows and then querying each one's children separately costs 101 round trips; use a JOIN or one batched IN query.
A leading wildcard like LIKE '%term' cannot use a normal B-tree index; use full-text search or a trigram index (pg_trgm) instead.
Every index speeds up reads but slows writes and uses disk; in PostgreSQL, pg_stat_user_indexes shows indexes with idx_scan = 0 that are never used.
In PostgreSQL, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds an index without blocking writes, which matters a lot on large production tables.
NULL never equals anything, even NULL: use IS NULL, and remember that NOT IN (subquery) returns no rows if the subquery yields any NULL.
curl -i prints response headers with the body, curl -I sends a HEAD request for headers only, and curl -v shows the full exchange including TLS.
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}\n' <url> prints only the status code and total time, great for quick latency checks.
curl --json '{"name":"a"}' <url> (curl 7.82+) POSTs JSON and sets Content-Type and Accept headers for you; older versions need -H and -d.
curl --resolve example.com:443:10.0.0.5 https://example.com tests one specific server IP while keeping the right Host header and TLS SNI.
In Chrome DevTools, right-click a request in the Network tab and choose Copy > Copy as cURL to replay it exactly from your terminal.
PUT and DELETE should be idempotent but POST is not; to make POST retries safe, send an idempotency key so duplicates are ignored.
HTTP 429 means you are rate limited; honor the Retry-After header and retry with exponential backoff plus random jitter.
Define hosts in ~/.ssh/config with Host, HostName, User, and IdentityFile, so ssh prod replaces a long command full of flags.
ssh -J bastion target (or ProxyJump bastion in ~/.ssh/config) hops through a bastion host transparently, and scp and git use it too.
ssh -L 5433:db.internal:5432 bastion forwards localhost:5433 to a private database that only the bastion can reach.
ControlMaster auto, ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%r@%h:%p, and ControlPersist 10m in ~/.ssh/config reuse one connection, making repeat ssh and git calls near instant.
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C 'you@example.com' creates a modern key that is shorter and faster than RSA; protect it with a passphrase.
On macOS, add UseKeychain yes and AddKeysToAgent yes to ~/.ssh/config so your key passphrase is stored in the Keychain.
Regex quantifiers are greedy: <.+> matches from the first < to the last >. Add ? for lazy matching, so <.+?> stops at the first >.
\b is a regex word boundary: \bcat\b matches 'cat' in 'the cat sat' but not inside 'concatenate'.
Named groups make regexes readable: (?<year>\d{4})-(?<month>\d{2}) in JavaScript, .NET, and PCRE; Python spells it (?P<year>\d{4}).
Lookaheads match without consuming: ^(?=.*\d)(?=.*[A-Z]).{8,}$ requires a digit, an uppercase letter, and at least 8 characters.
Nested quantifiers like (a+)+ can backtrack catastrophically on non-matching input (ReDoS); use tighter patterns or a linear-time engine like RE2.
Anchor validation regexes with ^ and $ (or \A and \z); without anchors, 'abc123' passes a check for \d+ because a match exists somewhere inside.
VS Code: Cmd-P opens files by fuzzy name; type > for commands, @ for symbols in the file, # for workspace symbols, and : to go to a line.
VS Code: F12 goes to definition, Shift-F12 lists references, F2 renames a symbol across files, and Ctrl-- jumps back to where you were.
VS Code: Cmd-D adds the next occurrence of the selection as another cursor, and Cmd-Shift-L selects every occurrence at once.
VS Code: Ctrl-` toggles the integrated terminal, and Cmd-\ splits the editor side by side.
JetBrains: press Shift twice for Search Everywhere to find any class, file, symbol, action, or setting.
JetBrains: Cmd-Shift-A (Find Action) runs any IDE command by name, so you never have to hunt through menus.
JetBrains on macOS: Cmd-E shows recent files, Cmd-B goes to declaration, and Option-F7 finds usages.
JetBrains Local History (right-click > Local History > Show History) recovers changes you never committed, even after a bad revert.
Never commit secrets: keep them in a secrets manager or environment, add .env to .gitignore, and run gitleaks or trufflehog in pre-commit or CI.
If a secret was ever pushed, rotate it immediately; deleting it in a new commit still leaves it in history, forks, and CI caches.
Use a password manager and a unique password for every site; credential stuffing attacks replay passwords leaked elsewhere.
Prefer passkeys or hardware security keys for 2FA; they resist phishing, while SMS codes are vulnerable to SIM swapping.
Least privilege: give services and CI tokens only the scopes they need, and set expiry dates on personal access tokens.
Commit lockfiles and review dependency updates; npm audit, pip-audit, and Dependabot flag versions with known vulnerabilities.
Build SQL with parameterized queries, never string concatenation; keeping data separate from code is what prevents SQL injection.
Before running curl ... | sh, download the script and read it first; prefer package managers that verify signed packages.
Write messages that stand alone: include context, the actual question, and what you tried, instead of sending just 'hi, got a minute?'
Lead with the conclusion (bottom line up front); many busy readers only read your first sentence.
Good bug reports include steps to reproduce, expected versus actual results, versions, and logs; they save a full round trip of questions.
Design docs should list the alternatives you considered and why you rejected them; that is what future readers need most.
Replace vague words with numbers: 'p99 latency rose from 120 ms to 900 ms after deploy 42' beats 'the API got slow'.
Record decisions and their reasons in the ticket or an ADR (architecture decision record); memory fades and chat threads get lost.
Timebox being stuck: after 30 to 60 minutes without progress, ask for help and share what you already tried.
Keep a brag document of wins, impact, and feedback as they happen; it makes reviews and promotion cases easy to write.
Read code from well-run open-source projects in your stack; it is one of the fastest ways to absorb idioms and design patterns.
defaults read com.apple.dock dumps an app's preferences; defaults write -g ApplePressAndHoldEnabled -bool false makes held keys repeat instead of showing the accent popup.
Spaced repetition apps like Anki are a proven way to retain commands, APIs, and concepts you want to remember long term.
Teach what you learn in a blog post, a lunch talk, or a doc; explaining a topic quickly exposes gaps in your understanding.
Protect deep work: batch notifications and block focus time on your calendar, since every interruption costs time to rebuild context.
Before starting a big task, write down what 'done' looks like; clear acceptance criteria prevent both scope creep and gold-plating.
The 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet (6 m) away for 20 seconds to reduce eye strain.
Use 1:1s for more than status updates: bring questions about growth, feedback, and the next step you want in your career.
